messages.subject: DIC in INLA and inlabru
parts:
Hello,

I am fitting LGCP models and want to compare them using the DIC.
When I fit the same models using INLA and inlabru, and they usually yield very similar results, but the DIC is really different.

I linked an example (based on https://becarioprecario.bitbucket.io/spde-gitbook/ch-lcox.html#introduction-1) where I fit both models. The intercept, range and sigma are almost identical, but the DIC is -727.6 with INLA, and -67.22 with inlabru.

How do we explain this and is one of the DIC more reliable?

Thank you!

Edgar

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] DIC in INLA and inlabru
parts:
Hi,

Due to the multitude of ways the point process likelihood can be implemented, E.g. with different integration schemes, and with different normalisation constants, one should not rely on raw DIC values. At best, differences in DIC between two models with _exactly_ the same likelihood implementation should be comparable.

 In your inla vs inlabru comparison, you probably used a different likelihood construction than the defaults of inlabru, explaining the difference.

In addition, the specific way in which the DIC values are computed/estimated can also make a difference. I hope to write more about this after going through the inla code and also doing the math properly for the different likelihood approximations.

Finn

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] DIC in INLA and inlabru
parts:
Hi,
Yes, if you’re using the dual mesh approach to manually construct an LGCP approximation in plain inla you’re not using the same method as inlabru. Inlabru uses the method from the Going off Grid paper, which (contrary to popular belief) does _not_ use the dual mesh (the plot of the dual mesh in the paper just illustrates the the basis functions have the same integrals as the areas in the dual mesh). The dual mesh approaches in some examples are lower order approximations.
In addition, inlabru by default combines all the log(lambda) terms into a single predictor likelihood contribution, which may affect how DIC is computed.  So you should be able to compare DIC between inla() models, and between bru() models, but not necessarily between inla&bru models unless you implement the inlabru method in inla() yourself.

Another difference, which might be the reason for differences, is that the default prior for the intercept is currently not the same in inla() and bru(). Set it explicitly with Intercept(1, prec.linear=…) to see if that changes things.

Finn

﻿Ive been busy, sorry.
You can see exactly how inlabru implements the point process likelihood (model=“cp”) in the code for the like() function (see the github repo for inlabru). The integration part is probably the same as you were doing in plain inla(). The “sum log lambda” part by default is a single likelihood contribution, whereas your implementation is likely separate contributions for each observed point, and potentially dual mesh aggregated counts instead of precise lambda(s) values, but I don’t remember if you specified that earlier in the thread.
Finn

Le lundi 26 février 2024 à 10:10:58 UTC-5, Finn Lindgren a écrit :
Hi,

Due to the multitude of ways the point process likelihood can be implemented, E.g. with different integration schemes, and with different normalisation constants, one should not rely on raw DIC values. At best, differences in DIC between two models with _exactly_ the same likelihood implementation should be comparable.

 In your inla vs inlabru comparison, you probably used a different likelihood construction than the defaults of inlabru, explaining the difference.

In addition, the specific way in which the DIC values are computed/estimated can also make a difference. I hope to write more about this after going through the inla code and also doing the math properly for the different likelihood approximations.

Finn
